title: The 1936 photo that sparked time travel theories: What is the mysterious man in New York holding?
excerpt: The 1936 photo that sparked time travel theories: What is the mysterious man in New York holding?
content:
Fun

Express newspaper

24/09/2026 11:55

A black-and-white photograph taken in New York in 1936 has resurfaced on social media after a small detail in the background sparked unusual time travel theories. The image shows a man holding what appears to be a cell phone-like device to his ear, almost five decades before such technology was available.

The photo shows several people walking through Union Square in Manhattan, but the attention of internet users has been drawn to a man in the foreground of the image.

He is seen with his back to the camera and appears to be holding an object near his ear.

This very detail has been enough to spark theories on social media that the photo may have captured a "time traveler" using a mobile phone.

Because the man was photographed from behind, the object he is holding is not clearly visible and it is impossible to identify with certainty.

"It looks like the man in the middle, in the front, is talking on his cell phone... Hmm, time travel?" one Facebook user commented.

Another asked: "Is this a time traveler talking on the phone right in front of us?"

Cell phones appeared decades later.

What makes the photo interesting is the fact that portable cell phones did not exist in 1936.

The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, widely considered the first commercially available portable mobile phone, only went on sale in 1983.

This happened a full 47 years after the photograph was taken.

However, skeptics have offered much more common explanations.

According to them, the man may have been carrying a shortwave radio receiver, a technology that has existed since the 1920s.

Due to its position and the quality of the photograph, the object remains unclear.

The photo was taken by Berenice Abbott.

The image was taken by renowned American photographer Berenice Abbott on July 16, 1936.

She photographed the Union Square area in Manhattan as part of her famous documentary project "Changing New York", carried out as part of the Federal Art Project.

The photograph is titled "Union Square, 14th Street and Broadway" and depicts one of the busiest intersections in New York City during the Great Depression.

The image is currently in the collection of the Brooklyn Museum.

Over the years, the photo has been shared repeatedly on social media, where users not only admire Abbott's documentary work but continue to speculate about the mystery man.

"I love that man in the vest talking on his cell phone," one Facebook user wrote.

Another joked, saying: "I'm almost sure it's Marty McFly," referring to the famous character from the movie "Back to the Future."

Another photograph from 1943 sparked similar theories.

This is not the first time a historical photograph has been interpreted as possible evidence of time travel.

Another black-and-white image, taken in Reykjavik, Iceland during World War II in 1943, sparked similar debate.

The photograph shows a man who appears to be holding something close to his ear, in a way that many social media users compared to modern mobile phone use.

Kristjan Hoffman, whose family had kept the photo for decades, posted it on Facebook.

"One thing that catches the eye in this beautiful photograph is that, above the window, in the corner in the middle of the image, a man is leaning and appears to be talking on a cell phone," he wrote.

The post caused immediate debate.

Some users thought the man really looked like he was talking on the phone, while others suggested he might just be scratching his ear or holding a watch next to him to check if it was working.

Hoffman, however, pushed the time travel theory even further.

According to him, the man seemed to stand out from the others and was wearing different clothes.

"He stands alone, has a different hat from the others, wears a scarf and behaves very similarly to us today," he said.

It could have been radio, but even this theory has problems.

The Iceland photo was originally published by Hoffman in 2016, but came back to the internet's attention years later.

On platform X, some users suggested that the man might be carrying a small radio.

However, small transistor radios did not come to market until the 1950s.

One user joked about the theory:

"A man scratches his ear and 83 years later is accused of being a time traveler."

Another highlighted the biggest problem with the cell phone theory.

"If there were no secret cell phone antennas, a cell phone would be completely useless at that time," he wrote.

This is also one of the main reasons why the theory of time travel is seen more as an internet curiosity than a realistic explanation.

Could he have been a spy?

Another theory has been put forward about the Iceland photograph.

Some have suggested that the man may have been a spy for the Axis powers during World War II and that the object he was carrying may have been a communications device.

Iceland officially maintained a neutral stance during the war, but was occupied by Allied forces due to its strategic position in the North Atlantic.

In 1940, the British took control of the island to prevent a possible German invasion.

Later, responsibility for the defense of Iceland was transferred to the United States.

This story has led some internet users to suggest alternative scenarios for the mysterious man, although there is no concrete evidence that he was a spy or used any unusual devices.

Mystery that continues to entertain the internet

The 1936 photograph remains an interesting example of how a small detail in a historical image can take on a whole new meaning in the age of social media.

There is no evidence that the man in Union Square was using a cell phone, much less that he was a time traveler.

The most likely explanations are related to a radio, a personal object, or simply a gesture that, from the angle of the photo, creates the illusion of using a telephone.

However, it is precisely the ambiguity of the image that continues to keep the story alive.

Nearly 90 years after the photo was taken, the mysterious man in Union Square continues to ignite the internet's imagination - even though time travel still remains a science fiction phenomenon and not a proven technology. /GazetaExpress/
